blocks: Ableton Live: Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record, Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Set Locator
Launchpad: a pad at Launchpad/UI/<Area>/Pad/<Name>; Launchpad/Custom/Mode/1 Arrangement describes one pad set up as a toggle.
A proposal for describing how a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control changes its value, apart from the protocol that carries it. Not yet a preference.
Form — what the control is physically or on screen: knob, button, pad, fader, field. The <Kind> segment of a control's page name records the form, in the product's own word.

Behavior — what happens to the value when the control is operated. The same form can behave in different ways: a Launchpad pad can be a toggle, a momentary button or a trigger, as in Launchpad/Custom/Mode/1 Arrangement.
MIDI is one way to carry a control's value to another device. A behavior describes the control itself; a MIDI CC number or a MIDI mapping goes under the control's Remote control block.
Momentary — on while held, off when released.
Trigger — fires one event when pressed and keeps no state, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Set Locator.
Toggle — alternates between two states on each press, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record.
Multi-state toggle — steps through three or more states in a fixed cycle on each press.
Unipolar — a value from zero up to a maximum, such as 0–127 or 0–100%.
Bipolar — a value centered on zero that runs from a negative minimum to a positive maximum, such as Length on Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/Sample/Length, from -100 to 100.
Relative (endless) — sends increments and decrements with no fixed end; the device keeps the value.
Selector — moves through a fixed list of named positions, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type.
Numeric field — holds a number typed in or dragged, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Field/Arrangement Position.
Encoder with push — a rotary control whose press acts as a separate button.
Pressure — adds a continuous value to a pad or key while held, such as aftertouch.
Position on a surface — a fader, slider or touch strip whose value follows a position along a line, or an XY pad that gives two values at once.
Whether each behavior gets its own page under this one, so a control page can link to it.
Whether a control page records its behavior in a property such as ui-control-behavior:: or in a body line.
How to model a control whose behavior depends on a mode, such as a knob that is bipolar in one oscillator model and unipolar in another.
In this garden, UI Control Setting pages model one mode a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control selects, one parameter that exists only in such a mode, or one gesture that gives the control another function.
A mode: one named position of a selector, such as the oscillator model Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog.
A parameter: the name another control takes while that mode is active, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog/Detune, which the Wave knob sets.

A gesture: a way of operating the control other than its plain use, such as pressing a knob, holding a button, or using the control while Shift is held: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/06 Save Button/Hold.
A plain value along a range, such as 64 on a knob, is not a setting page.
A mode sits at <Control>/<Mode>, beneath the control that selects it; a parameter sits at <Control>/<Mode>/<Parameter>.
A gesture sits at <Control>/<Gesture>, named Press, Hold or Shift. A gesture that combines two nests the second beneath the first: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/02 Paraphonic Button/Hold/Shift.
Use the names the display or manual shows.
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Control/Setting]] and up:: to the control or mode above it; prev:: and next:: follow the order of modes in the manual when the modes are numbered.
One bullet-wrapped H1, then one sentence on what the setting does.
A parameter page names the control that sets it, with a link.
A Source line links the user guide or manual section.
In this garden, UX Pattern pages model reusable interaction patterns and interface affordances that describe how an interface behaves, how people invoke it, and what kind of action space it opens up.
A page under UX/Pattern/... is a strong candidate for this entity type, but the namespace alone does not decide the type.
Neighboring UX/... pages may still be better modeled as term or concept pages when they are mainly a definition, essay, or design lens rather than a reusable interaction pattern.
Good fit: recurring interface behaviors such as UX/Pattern/Dark, UX/Pattern/Text Input/Slash Command, and UX/Pattern/Text Input/Suggest/Completion.
Good fit: patterns whose primary identity is the interaction itself, not one vendor's implementation.
Not this type: tool-specific notes such as Claude/Code/Command/Slash when the page is mainly about one product's feature surface rather than the general pattern.
Prefer concept when the page is a broader design or ethics explanation.
Prefer term when the page is only a short vocabulary anchor.
Search for an existing page before creating a new UX pattern entity.
Search in this order: exact expected title, alias matches, sibling branches under UX/Pattern/, product-specific pages that may be describing the same interaction, then page-body mentions.
Classify as: existing, similar (needs human judgment), new, or blocked.
On instances, set logseq-entity:: to this entity-type page so backlinks list all UX pattern entities.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Prefer singular, Title Case namespace segments.
Use nested paths when the host surface or interaction family adds useful structure, for example UX/Pattern/Text Input/Slash Command.
Keep cross-cutting patterns top-level when they are not tied to one host surface, for example UX/Pattern/Dark.
Use alias:: for legacy titles, common shorthand, or alternate surface forms such as Slash Command or Autocomplete.
Use a lean hub shape: H1 with the pattern name, then brief sections such as Overview, Interaction, Examples, and Related as the topic warrants.
Keep examples concrete and product-facing, but keep the page centered on the reusable interaction pattern rather than one implementation.

In this garden, Website pages model a specific published website treated as a thing in its own right — a site notable for its design, craft, experience, or usefulness, rather than for being one person's homepage or one codebase.
Website/Misato Town — a WebGL town-rebranding microsite by , notable for scroll-driven keyframed animation.
When we treat something as a website
Strong signals: a live site at a stable URL, cited for its design or experience; a showcase or award entry (e.g. ); a site whose identity is the site itself, not merely the org or product behind it.
When we treat something as a website

Not this type: a single post, essay, or article → Logseq/Entity/Article. A codebase, app, or tool that happens to have a URL → Logseq/Entity/Software/Project. The organization or company behind a site → Logseq/Entity/Organization or Logseq/Entity/Company. A person's personal site, which lives as a sub-page of that person, e.g. Person/Name/Web.
When we treat something as a website
A page may model more than one entity when it genuinely qualifies (see Logseq/Entity on multiple membership) — e.g. a site that is also the primary page for its software project.
When we treat something as a website
How to name the main page for a website
When the site's maker (studio, org, person) already has a namespace in the garden, use Creator/Website/<Short Name> so the site nests under its maker.
How to name the main page for a website
Otherwise use Website/<Name> as the fallback, where <Name> is the site's own recognizable name, e.g. Website/Misato Town.
How to name the main page for a website
Prefer the site's own short name over its full URL or a slug; put alternate names or the native-language title in alias::.
How to name the main page for a website
Check in this order: Website/<Name>, Creator/Website/<Name>, aliases, the maker's namespace, and body mentions of the URL. Classify as: existing, similar, new, or blocked.
Set logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Website]] to mark a page as a website instance. Additive — list comma-separated with any other entities, primary first (see Logseq/Entity).
created-by:: — link to the studio, company, or person that made the site, when tracked in the garden.
date-created:: — when the site launched or was published, not when the page was added.
Optional: logseq-created-time-year:: linking to the matching Logseq/Entity/Time/Year instance.
via:: records how the site was discovered (e.g. ); see-also:: links genuinely related pages such as the collection it belongs to.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
First block: H1 with a Markdown link to the site's live URL.
Keep it lean: what the site is, why it is notable, the techniques or stack that matter, its maker, and any awards. Curated collections of sites are modeled by Logseq/Entity/Website/Collection.

In this garden, Website Collection pages model a specialization of the Logseq/Entity/Collection pattern: a curated collection of websites gathered around a theme or standard. Members are Logseq/Entity/Website instances.
Design/Good/Web — a curated gallery of exemplary web design, sitting under the broader Design/Good hub.
When a page might be modeling a website collection

Strong signals: a named, intentional selection of sites chosen for a shared quality (great design, a genre, a reference set); the page's job is the curation itself, and each member is a Logseq/Entity/Website.
When a page might be modeling a website collection

Not this type: a single site (use Logseq/Entity/Website); a heterogeneous design hub whose members are not all websites (keep as a plain hub page, e.g. Design/Good, per Logseq/Entity/Collection on typed members).
When a page might be modeling a website collection

Name the collection for its curating theme, nesting under an existing hub where one fits, e.g. Design/Good/Web. The reserved trailing /Collection marker is not required on instance names when the theme already reads as a collection; see Logseq/Entity/Collection.
Set logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Website/Collection]]. Additive — list comma-separated with any other entities, primary first (see Logseq/Entity).
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Lean: a line on what the collection curates and by what criterion, then a member list where each Logseq/Entity/Website gets a one-line note on why it belongs.
In this garden, Wishlist pages model a shortlist of features wanted for one particular tool or technology — candidates for a future upstream issue, PR, or config workaround.
When we treat something as a Wishlist entity
Strong signals: one page per technology under that technology's namespace ending in /Wishlist; the body is a curated shortlist of desired features, not a full product roadmap or issue tracker mirror.
When we treat something as a Wishlist entity

Not a Wishlist: a single feature request filed only as a Logseq/Entity/Question; a general notes page; a Logseq/Entity/Collection specialization (wishlist items are desires, not instances of another entity type — though an item may link a related Question).
When we treat something as a Wishlist entity
Link shape: [[Scope/Wishlist]] where Scope is the tool or technology page (e.g. tuicr/Wishlist, gh-dash/Wishlist).
File shape: pages/Scope___Wishlist.md with triple underscores between namespace parts.
One Wishlist page per technology. Do not invent a second wishlist under the same scope; add features as H2 sections on the existing page.
Grep for Wishlist under the technology's namespace prefix.
Classify as existing when that scope already has a Wishlist; new when the scope has none; similar when a differently named wants/ideas page covers the same tool.
On new Wishlist pages, include logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/Wishlist]].
Optional see-also:: only for surprising adjacent garden pages (not the parent technology the title already encodes).
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
H1 — Wishlist (the namespace already names the technology).
First child — one short sentence: upstream feature ideas for [[Scope]], optionally naming the upstream repo.
One H2 per wanted feature — concise feature name as the heading.
Prefer a child link to a related Logseq/Entity/Question when the gap was researched as a Q.
One H2 per wanted feature — concise feature name as the heading.
Wanted: what the feature should do.
One H2 per wanted feature — concise feature name as the heading.
Today: what exists instead (or that nothing does).
One H2 per wanted feature — concise feature name as the heading.
Keep the list short — a shortlist, not an exhaustive backlog. Drop or archive items once shipped upstream or deliberately declined.
Question: a Wishlist item often points at a Scope/Q/… page that recorded the research; the Wishlist is the standing shortlist, the Question is the answered (or open) inquiry.
Software Project / Plugin / CLI tool pages: the technology hub may link its Wishlist under a small wishlist child; the Wishlist remains a separate entity page.
In this garden, YouTube Video pages model one identifiable video published on YouTube.
The YouTube video ID is the deduplication key. Search youtube.com/watch?v=<id> and youtu.be/<id> across pages before creating a page, regardless of title, channel, or page namespace.

A page that merely embeds or cites a video while documenting another subject is not a YouTube Video instance. A raw transcript child page is part of its parent video's notes, not a second video entity.

Prefer <creator>/YouTube/<YY>/<MM>/<short title> when the publishing creator and publication month are known. The creator may be a person, company, organization, or software project. Preserve an established video page's path when marking an existing instance.
A video in an ordered run can instead live beneath a series hub, with a published ordinal before its short title. Logseq/Entity/Series governs ordinals and ordering.
logseq-entity:: with Logseq/Entity/YouTube marks a video. Add Logseq/Entity/Series after it when the video is an installment of an ordered series.

Record date-created:: from the video's publication date when verifiable. Link its known year through logseq-created-time-year:: to a matching Logseq/Entity/Time/Year page. Shared property conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Lead with a bullet-wrapped H1 that links to the video's watch URL. Name the publisher or speaker when known; keep any synopsis and notes beneath the heading.
A {{video ...}} block is useful when inline playback or timestamped notes are part of the page. Notes with clickable {{youtube-timestamp ...}} headings nest beneath that video block.

When a video is also a podcast episode, its page lists Logseq/Entity/Podcast/Episode first in logseq-entity::. That page holds the shape for the combination: video seconds for every timestamp, chapters as headings, snips, highlights, and frames for what only the video shows.
A YouTube playlist is a separate entity modeled by Logseq/Entity/YouTube/Playlist. A video's playlist membership does not change its video identity.
In this garden, YouTube Playlist pages model one identifiable playlist published on YouTube.
The YouTube list ID is the deduplication key. Search playlist URLs and existing hub pages before creating a second page for a different name for the same playlist.
An informal list of video links without a YouTube playlist ID is a collection or series, but not a YouTube Playlist instance.

An ordered playlist declares logseq-entity:: with Logseq/Entity/YouTube/Playlist first and Logseq/Entity/Series second. The playlist hub is the one external work and the named sequence; member videos remain distinct Logseq/Entity/YouTube pages.

Prefer a hub near its member videos, often <creator>/YouTube/Series/<name>; retain a requested or established path when it is already the series hub. Put a published ordinal on members only when the playlist or publisher uses one.

Shared property conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter. Add a verifiable date-created:: and creation-year link when the playlist's own creation date is known; the date of its oldest video does not establish the playlist's creation date.
Lead with a bullet-wrapped H1 linked to the playlist URL. Describe the scope briefly and list member video page links in playlist order when known.

I was working on logseq flashcard review today in in Logseq/Flashcard/Review with {{cards ( or [[rg]] [[vim]] [[nvim]] [[fzf]] [[Zoxide]] [[yazi]] [[tmux]] [[Lazygit]] [[Lightroom/Classic]] )}} and I came across a few flashcards that were blank. I couldn't advance beyond them.

Cause: empty outline bullets (- with no text) nested under otherwise valid #card / [[card]] blocks. Review walks child blocks; those steps had no renderable body, so the UI showed blank “slides” and felt like a hard stop until each step was graded.

Repo fix: a deck-scoped scan (same or link set as on Logseq/Flashcard/Review, matching ancestor [[…]] text plus obvious hub filenames) found two cards with stray empty children: Lightroom/Classic/Keyshort/Managing Photos and Catalogs/Show in Explorer and Finder (two trailing empty bullets) and tmux/Keyshort/Pane/Rotate Panes (one trailing empty bullet). Those bullets were removed; a repeat scan reports zero empty bullets under matching deck cards.

Coverage check: no matching deck card lacked a substantive answer subtree (ignoring card-*:: lines). The [[nvim]] disjunct did not match any cards by ancestry that the other query links did not already cover (everything in this pass was already tied to another scope link or hub filename).

Docs / tooling: Logseq docs clone at ~/Documents/GitHub/logseq/docs — pages/Flashcards.md, pages/Queries.md. nbb was not on PATH in the environment used; verification used a small Python outline pass (tab depth, #card / [[card]], walk deeper bullets until outdent) instead of an NBB-Logseq script.
